title: Without a Paddle
full_review:
Three friends set out on a canoeing expedition in search of hidden treasure but wind up discovering something much more valuable in the only fitfully funny "Without a Paddle" (Paramount).

The movie is one of those late-summer, scrapheap releases that studios tend to pull out of the bottom of the mortar bin after having already fired all their rounds of heavy blockbuster ammunition.

The story orbits around three lifelong buddies: Dan (Seth Green), a successful but slightly neurotic doctor; Jerry (Matthew Lillard), a corporate slacker with commitment issues; and Tom (Dax Shepard), a freewheeling easy-rider. Prompted by the untimely death of their fourth amigo, Billy (Anthony Starr), the trio decides to make good on a childhood pact to find DB Cooper's $200,000 in stolen loot which was lost when the infamous airline hijacker parachuted into the Oregon wilderness (and quite possibly to his death) in 1971.

The by-the-numbers film follows a predictable whatever-can-go-wrong-does formula, as the three stooges try to "rough it" in the wilderness. During their trip downriver they must navigate a whitewater gauntlet of low-comedy rapids -- none of which is particularly funny -- including run-ins with a maternally minded grizzly, a couple of heavily armed backwoods marijuana farmers and a pair of tree-hugging hippie chicks in desperate need of leg waxing. Along the way, there are enough breaks in the action for the musketeers to learn schmaltzy all-for-one-and-one-for-all lessons about friendship and finding purpose in life.

Burt Reynolds -- who knows a thing or two about the dangers involved in river runs -- makes a late entrance as an eccentric mountain man, providing yet another, sigh, comic connection to "Deliverance."

As directed by Steven Brill, the laugh-lite film is full of gross-out sight gags, generally of the scatological, stoner and slapstick variety (or some combination of the three). Examples include the flower power twins aiding the boys in an escape by torpedoing their redneck pursuers with brown-bag bombs of excrement.

But, while this film is up the creek without much of a narrative paddle, it does come equipped with a surprisingly moral compass -- though for much of the movie's 99 minutes its needle has a hard time finding a truly tasteful North. If you look past its forced frat-house humor -- which, admittedly, is asking a lot -- you can glean some positive nuggets. In one of the film's several attempts at genuine emotion, Jerry, enlightened by a newfound sense of direction and appreciation for his friends, exclaims "Being alive, that's the treasure"; a simple statement, at once both prosaic and profound. Not a bad message coming from an otherwise mindless movie.

Due to a few sexual encounters, drug content, some violence as well as recurring coarse language and crude humor, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
